sql.summary: Speaks SQL at all. Redis does not.

transactions.summary: BEGIN / COMMIT / ROLLBACK against a pinned connection.

databaseSelect.summary: A default database can be chosen for the editor (USE / search_path / a request parameter).

processList.summary: A server-side list of running work that can be inspected and killed.

serverInfo.summary: Server settings and status are readable.

sqlDba.summary: The catalog-driven DBA panels: tuner rule sets, replication topology, ANALYZE, locks, GRANTs, saved SQL, the playground, schema compare, the documenter, whole-schema value search.

lockWaits.summary: Blocking chains can be read: who waits on whom, for how long, on what.
detail: Split out of `sqlDba` because that flag gates fifteen panels at once, and those panels are not one feature — they are fifteen, each needing its own catalog queries per engine. SQL Server can do blocking chains today (`sys.dm_os_waiting_tasks`) while it still cannot do, say, the documenter, so a single flag could only be wrong in one direction or the other: fifteen hidden panels, or fifteen broken ones.

This also gates the Locks & Deadlocks panel's deadlock tab (wait-for graph + incident history): the three engines that publish anything about deadlocks — SQL Server's system_health graph history, MySQL's latest detected deadlock, PostgreSQL's per-database counters — are exactly the three with blocking chains, so the old separate `deadlocks` flag could only ever echo this one and was folded into it.
Expect more of these as SQL Server gains the rest — see plan-sqlserver.md Phase 2. Each one is added when the panel behind it actually works.

sequences.summary: Sequences exist as objects that can be listed, created and altered.
detail: Not `sqlDba`, for the same reason as `lockWaits`. Note this is *not* the same set as the SQL engines: MySQL proper has no sequences at all (AUTO_INCREMENT is a column property), while MariaDB, PostgreSQL and SQL Server do — so the panel is gated on the object existing, not on the engine family. MySQL-vs-MariaDB is decided at runtime from the server flavour, which a static table cannot express; this flag says "ask", and `SequencePanel` says "MySQL has none" when the flavour comes back plain.

longQueryWatch.summary: A watchdog can list running statements server-wide, with age, and kill one.
detail: Distinct from `processList`, which is the raw list: this is the watcher that ages entries against a threshold and alerts. Needs a per-statement elapsed time and the statement text, which ClickHouse and the file engines do not offer in that shape.

replication.summary: A primary/replica topology this panel can draw: replicas that report a log position and a lag.
detail: Split from `sqlDba` because SQL Server replicates but does **not** fit that shape — Always On availability groups are per-database, with a synchronisation state and a redo queue rather than a byte offset. That gap is registered in `utils/engineGaps.ts` and shown greyed with the reason instead of being silently absent.

columnProfile.summary: A column can be profiled: nulls, distinct counts, extremes, value lengths.
detail: Needs only ordinary aggregates and a row-count estimate, so it is set for every engine with a real catalog and cheap row counts.

dbSearch.summary: Every table in a schema can be searched for a value.
detail: Needs a catalog to enumerate columns and a LIKE with an escape clause — which all three SQL engines have, in three different spellings.

findUsages.summary: Where a table or column is referenced by the server's own SQL — views, routines, triggers, constraints, defaults, and whatever else the engine stores a definition for.
detail: Needs a catalog that hands back the *text* of those definitions, which the three SQL engines do in three different ways (`SHOW CREATE`, `pg_get_*def`, `OBJECT_DEFINITION`).

dataCompare.summary: Two tables can be compared row by row, across sessions, and a reconciliation script generated.
detail: Both sides must be the SAME engine — the panel filters the session list on it — because the generated INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE is written in one dialect, and the value representations have to agree before a diff means anything.

documenter.summary: A schema can be documented: columns, types, keys, indexes, foreign keys, routines and whatever comments the engine stores.

routines.summary: Stored routines can be listed, read, edited and saved.
detail: The write is the reason this is its own flag: the panel replaces a live procedure. MySQL has to DROP then CREATE and keeps the original in hand to restore; PostgreSQL and SQL Server replace in one statement (`CREATE OR REPLACE`, `CREATE OR ALTER`) and cannot leave a hole. An engine that cannot do one of those safely does not belong here.

userAdmin.summary: Accounts and their permissions can be listed and edited.
detail: Editing means *generating* SQL for review — this panel never executes a write — but the engine still has to have a security model TxUI can read back and diff against, which is why it is not simply `sqlDba`.

fleet.summary: A label's servers can be compared with each other.
detail: Needs three things the engine must actually have: a name/value settings catalogue, a listable index set, and a per-table statistics timestamp. Without the last one the panel's third tab is permanently empty, which is why this is not simply `sqlDba`.

playground.summary: A contention scenario can be manufactured on this server.
detail: Needs N real, concurrent server sessions and a way to make them queue on a row — so an in-process engine cannot do it however much SQL it speaks, and an engine without row locks has nothing to demonstrate.

namespaceDdl.summary: Namespaces (schemas / databases) can be created and dropped from the tree.
detail: Its own flag rather than `sqlDba` because the three engines that have them spell every part differently — `IF NOT EXISTS` does not exist on SQL Server, `CASCADE` is PostgreSQL's alone, and `CREATE SCHEMA` must lead its own batch in T-SQL. An engine here needs a real builder in `utils/schemaObjSql.ts`, not a generic one.

stmtStats.summary: Cumulative per-statement statistics can be snapshotted and diffed over time — "which statements got slower between these two moments".
detail: Needs a server-side, cumulative statement digest keyed by a stable id. MySQL has `performance_schema.events_statements_summary_by_digest` (requires performance_schema, on by default), PostgreSQL has `pg_stat_statements` (an extension — the panel detects it and offers to enable it). SQL Server's Query Store is richer than a diff (plan history and forcing — see `queryStore`) and keeps its own panel, so it is deliberately not here.

queryStore.summary: The engine keeps a HISTORY of query plans, and can be told to use one.
detail: Not "has query statistics" — MySQL's digests and PostgreSQL's `pg_stat_statements` both have those, and neither keeps a plan or can pin it. This flag means the two things that make a regression actionable: every plan a query has had, and `sp_query_store_force_plan`.

maintenance.summary: The Maintenance panel: table upkeep — CHECK / ANALYZE / OPTIMIZE / REPAIR, plus the invalid-objects scan — and, on SQLite, file upkeep (VACUUM, integrity checks, ANALYZE). ANALYZE is the one WRITE in the read-only DBA set: the panel pre-flights the server's read-only state before running it (`super_read_only`, `pg_is_in_recovery()`, `DATABASEPROPERTYEX(…, 'Updateability')`). Broader than `sqlDba`, which SQLite lacks.

erDiagram.summary: Foreign keys and a schema graph exist to draw.

dataGen.summary: Rows can be generated and inserted.

csvImport.summary: CSV can be loaded into a table.

sqlQuality.summary: The SQL quality audit (EXPLAIN + statistics + index advice).

sqlVariables.summary: Statements can be parameterised with `:name` variables before running.

writes.summary: Anything can be written at all.

tableDesigner.summary: The table designer can serve this engine — it has CREATE/ALTER TABLE DDL the designer models. True for the four SQL engines that own real tables; Redis has no tables and Parquet has nothing to write to.

statementTimeout.summary: A server-side ceiling on a single statement can be set.
detail: True does not mean it covers writes — on MySQL it does not. See `DEFAULT_STATEMENT_TIMEOUT_SECS` in the backend.
